Amortization is fine and 180 kernels is a lot, but neither matters if the overhead being removed is tiny. Measure the fraction first.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: You switch from a BERT-based reranker to an XLM-RoBERTa-based one and keep the same max_length. Which detail changes in packing?
options: The query is now placed after the document
There are no special tokens at all
The model accepts 1,024 positions automatically
The pair uses four special tokens and no segment ids, so one fewer document token fits
explain: XLM-RoBERTa packs a pair as <s> A </s></s> B </s> and does not use token type ids. Order and the max_length you pass stay the same; the budget for the document shrinks by one token.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: A colleague proposes caching cross-encoder scores for every (query, document) pair to remove reranking latency. When does this actually help?
options: Only for repeated exact queries (head queries) over an unchanged candidate set; the long tail of new queries still pays full cost
Always, because cross-encoder scores never change
Never, because the scores depend on batch size
Only if the model uses sigmoid outputs
explain: A score is a function of the exact query and document text. Caching works for frequent repeated queries, which Hofstatter et al. also note as the exception, but most queries in real traffic are unique and must be scored live.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
question: Why does a one-time pad not replace AES for HTTPS (encrypted web traffic)?
options: Because XOR is too slow on modern CPUs
Because the key must be as long as all the traffic and delivered securely in advance
Because it was broken by quantum computers
Because it cannot encrypt binary data
explain: The pad is unbreakable but its key logistics are impossible at internet scale. Practical ciphers use a short key (16 or 32 bytes) and accept security based on computational difficulty.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound
question: Roughly how many random inputs until a collision is likely for a 160-bit hash such as SHA-1, if the hash were ideal?
explain: Birthday bound: about 2^(n/2) = 2^80. Real attacks on SHA-1 do better than that by exploiting its structure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster
question: Which Python call should generate a password-reset token?
options: random.getrandbits(128)
secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
uuid.uuid1()
hash(time.time())
explain: secrets reads the OS CSPRNG. random is predictable from its state or seed, uuid1 encodes time and the machine address, and hashing the time adds no entropy.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
question: A teammate proposes encrypting session cookies with AES-CTR and a counter stored in memory that resets to 0 on restart. Which rule does this break?
options: Do not hash passwords
Never reuse a nonce: after a restart the same counter values repeat under the same key, and CTR also lacks authentication
Use constant-time comparison
Retire SHA-1
explain: A counter that resets repeats keystreams (two-time pad), and plain CTR gives no integrity, so cookies could be bit-flipped. Use an AEAD with random or persistent nonces, or a vetted token library.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
question: Why do GMMA atoms on Hopper give every thread the whole A tile in their A layout instead of splitting it across threads?
options: Because Hopper has no registers for operands
Because wgmma reads A and B from shared memory through a descriptor built on the whole tile
Because CuTe cannot partition across 128 threads
To make every thread load A from global memory
explain: The docs explain that the GMMA descriptor is built on the full A or B tile in shared memory, so the ALayout maps every thread to the same tile (stride 0 in the thread mode) and CuTe checks that the shared memory layout is valid for a descriptor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
question: Which statement about a CPU write to CXL memory is correct?
options: The OS takes a page fault and copies the page to the device
The device DMA engine pulls the data from host memory
Writes must use special non-temporal instructions
The store goes into the CPU cache; when the dirty line is later evicted, the host sends an RwD and the device replies with an NDR
explain: CXL.mem is plain cache-coherent memory from the core's point of view. Stores land in the cache; the eviction of a dirty line becomes a request-with-data message, acknowledged by a no-data response.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
question: A client signs a test agreement covering 'all our cloud servers'. One server in the list is actually run by a hosting company on shared hardware. What is the right move?
options: Test it: the client listed it, so it is in scope
Confirm ownership and get the hosting provider's terms or consent before testing anything that is not the client's to authorise
Test it gently, at night, so nobody notices
Skip the agreement and rely on the bug bounty rules of the hosting company
explain: Only someone entitled to control a system can authorise access to it. A client's list proves what the client believes, not what it owns. Many cloud providers publish their own testing policies; read them and keep the result with the agreement.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
question: Under CMA section 5, which fact alone gives a section 1 offence a significant link to England and Wales?
options: The accused speaks English
The target server was in England at the time, even if the accused was abroad
The website uses a .uk domain name
The victim company is listed on the London Stock Exchange
explain: Section 5(2) gives two links for section 1: the accused was in the home country when acting, or the computer containing the targeted program or data was. A domain name or a listing is not on the list.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
question: A researcher in the US emails exploit details for a router bug to the router vendor's security team abroad, so they can fix it. Which concept in the 2021 BIS rule fits best?
options: Deemed export to an E:1 country
Vulnerability disclosure
Entity List designation
Intrusion software production
explain: The rule defines vulnerability disclosure as identifying, reporting or communicating a vulnerability to people responsible for remediating it, to resolve it. The 2017 Wassenaar change excluded such technology exchanges from the development-technology control.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
question: Why could Sullivan be convicted of misprision of a felony?
options: Because Uber's bug bounty programme was illegal
Because a security officer must publish every bug
Because the evidence showed the hackers committed a CFAA felony, Sullivan knew it, and took steps to conceal it instead of reporting it
Because the hackers were from another country
explain: The Ninth Circuit explained that misprision needs a completed felony by the principal (here unauthorised access under the CFAA), knowledge of it, and concealment. The NDA could not retroactively authorise the access.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The domain-weight update, step by step
question: A colleague's DoReMi port returns the domain weights from the final step instead of the average over steps. What is the likely effect?
options: The output is noisier and reflects only the end of training, while the method (following Nemirovski et al.) returns the average over the trajectory
None, because the weights converge to a fixed point after a few steps
Weights will no longer sum to 1
The proxy model will diverge
explain: Per-step weights react to one minibatch and keep moving as the proxy learns. The paper returns the average over all T steps, which is smoother and integrates the whole run, including the early phase when weights change most.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
question: Your linear regression over 5 domains recommends putting 100 percent of the budget on Wikipedia. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Wikipedia really is the best data and the other domains add nothing
A linear function over mixtures always has its minimum at a corner, so the pick reflects the model's form, not the data
The regression has too many runs and is overfitting
The proxy models were too large
explain: A linear function on the probability simplex is minimized at a vertex, a single-domain mixture. Mixture effects are nonlinear (the first few percent of a domain matter most), which is why RegMix prefers LightGBM and averages the top 100 predicted mixtures.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
question: Your GitHub domain is full of auto-generated config files. Which tool addresses this directly?
options: DoReMi, by lowering GitHub's domain weight
A document-level quality filter that drops low-value files inside the domain
Raising the smoothing parameter c
Iterated DoReMi with more rounds
explain: DoReMi can only scale the whole GitHub domain up or down, which also cuts the good code. Removing specific bad documents is a curation job, like phi-1's educational-value classifier.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: A teammate measures one cold lookup and finds SoA only 16% faster, so they conclude the split is pointless. What is the strongest reply?
options: The measurement must be wrong; SoA is always 4x faster here
Per-lookup misses are similar, but the searched data is 4x smaller, so across many lookups it stays cached and the gap widens
SoA only helps with SIMD, and binary search is not vectorized
They should switch to a linked list of keyframes
explain: A single cold lookup misses in both layouts on its first few probes. The benefit of a 512-byte index over a 2 KiB one shows up when many lookups reuse the same lines, which is how an animation system runs.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
question: A system stores public product photos (confidentiality not applicable, integrity LOW, availability LOW) and customer support chats (confidentiality MODERATE, integrity LOW, availability LOW). What is its FIPS 199 confidentiality?
options: NOT APPLICABLE, because most of its data is public
LOW, the average
MODERATE, the highest value among its information types
HIGH, because it is customer-facing
explain: FIPS 199 uses the high-water mark: the system's value for each objective is the highest among its information types. Volume and averages do not matter; the support chats set confidentiality to MODERATE.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
question: An attacker steals the full orders database of a shop that uses vault tokenisation. What do they get for card numbers?
options: The card numbers, because the token is an encoding of them
Random tokens that only the vault can map back to card numbers
Card numbers, but only the last four digits
Encrypted card numbers they can brute-force offline
explain: Vault tokens are random and the mapping lives only in the vault, so there is nothing to decode or brute-force in the stolen table. Vaultless tokens (FPE, AES-SIV) are different: anyone with the key can reverse them.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Where DLP acts: endpoints, email, web and cloud
question: Why deploy a new DLP blocking rule in simulation mode first?
options: Simulation mode is faster
Because blocking rules are illegal in some countries
To measure how often it would fire and on what, and tune precision, before it blocks legitimate work
Simulation mode encrypts the data
explain: Simulation applies no actions but records matches, so you can measure false positives on real traffic and fix the detector or scope. Turning blocking on first usually breaks business processes and drives users to unmonitored channels.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
question: Which pairing of case and missing control is right?
options: Tea 2025: no TLS on uploads
Snowflake 2024: no field-level encryption
OPM 2015: no data classification
Morgan Stanley: no per-device certificate review or serial reconciliation
explain: Morgan Stanley's failures were vendor oversight, unreviewed certificates and missing inventory. Tea's was retention not enforced; the Snowflake thefts used valid credentials without MFA or network allow lists; at OPM, officials said encryption would not have stopped attackers with valid credentials.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
question: Your equivalence test asserts allclose on the logits with atol = 1e-3 and it passes. What has it established about the generated tokens?
options: They must be identical, since the logits agree to within 1e-3.
Very little on its own: a 1e-3 tolerance only protects an argmax whose top-2 margin exceeds 2e-3, and near-ties are far smaller than that.
They are identical as long as the temperature is 0.
Nothing, because allclose is never a valid comparison for logits.
explain: A tolerance d on logits preserves the top-2 ordering only when the gap exceeds 2d. With atol = 1e-3 the test is blind to every position whose margin is under 2e-3, and near-ties can be around 1e-06. A tolerance is usable when it is paired with the margin distribution; the problem is the missing margin check, not allclose itself.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
question: A teammate sets the network drop rate to 50% in every simulation run to "find more bugs". What is the likely effect?
options: More bugs found, since more faults always means more coverage
The cluster rarely makes progress, so the run explores a small, repetitive set of states
Determinism breaks, because drops are random
Nothing, because consensus tolerates any drop rate
explain: The FoundationDB paper explicitly tunes fault distributions to avoid an excessive fault rate that drives the system into a small state space. At 50% loss on every run the cluster mostly retries and times out; deep states such as long recoveries under load are rarely reached. Vary the rate per run instead.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
question: In the fixed workflow, why does the deploy job also need the production environment, when it already has `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`?
options: The `if:` is cosmetic and GitHub ignores it
Environments make jobs run faster
The `if:` lives in the workflow file, which a branch can edit; the environment's branch rule and reviewers are enforced by GitHub outside the file, and the cloud role can require that environment
Environments are needed to use actions/checkout
explain: A condition written in the workflow is only as trustworthy as the file. A branch can delete it. Environment protection rules are settings the branch cannot change, and an OIDC trust on environment:production means the cloud refuses tokens from any other job.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: OIDC from CI, precisely: subject claims and environments
question: A job runs on a pull_request event and references the environment `staging`. What subject does GitHub put in its token?
options: repo:ORG/REPO:pull_request
repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/pull/1/merge
repo:ORG/REPO:environment:staging
repo:ORG/REPO
explain: GitHub's reference: the subject includes the environment name when the job references an environment, and includes pull_request only if the job does not reference one.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Scanners in the pipeline: Checkov, Trivy and zizmor
question: A developer adds `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_24` with no comment to silence the open-SSH finding. What should the pipeline enforce?
options: Nothing: skips are always fine
Delete all skip comments automatically
Disable CKV_AWS_24 everywhere
Skips must name a reason (and ideally an owner and an end date) and go through review like any exception
explain: Checkov's format includes a suppression comment after the check id. A skip without a reason is an unreviewed exception to policy.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
question: A self-hosted runner is suspected of running attacker code. What is the right first containment step?
options: Delete suspicious files on it and keep using it
Take it offline and replace it from a clean image, then rotate every secret jobs on it could reach
Restart the runner service
Rename the runner
explain: A persistent runner can hide leftover processes and modified tools (the PyTorch case). Rebuilding from a known-good image is the only state you can trust; secrets that passed through it must be treated as stolen.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
question: LLaDA 8B Instruct, under pure diffusion sampling, gives very short answers on math benchmarks. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model was trained with a causal mask
The response length hyperparameter was set too large
Random remasking was used by default
Fine-tuning data padded with |EOS| makes tail |EOS| predictions highly confident, so low-confidence remasking commits them first
explain: Padding teaches the model that the tail is |EOS|, and low-confidence remasking commits the most confident tokens first. The fixes LLaDA used were to zero the |EOS| confidence or to sample block by block.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
question: Why does DiffuLLaMA keep the 'shift operation' when it turns LLaMA into a diffusion model?
options: Because bidirectional attention cannot work without it
Because the shift makes the KV cache exact
So that the pretrained output at position i keeps predicting the token at i + 1, reusing what the AR weights already learned
Because masked tokens must always be predicted from the right
explain: An AR model's hidden state at i is trained to encode the next token. Keeping that alignment means a masked token is read from its left neighbour's output, so continued training starts close to what the weights already do. Attention is fully bidirectional either way, and caching is unaffected.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
question: An offline batch job summarizes millions of documents overnight. There is no latency SLO; the goal is tokens per dollar. Which design do the sources point toward?
options: Separate prefill and decode clusters on different GPU generations, mandatory for throughput
Colocated serving with chunked prefill to keep every iteration near the compute-bound point
Disaggregation over 25 Gb/s Ethernet to save NVLink
Disaggregation, because it always raises goodput
explain: Goodput only matters when there are SLOs. DistServe's discussion says that in throughput-oriented offline settings, chunked prefill with piggybacking (decode tokens riding along in the batch of each prefill chunk) may be preferred because it fills each batch to the compute-bound threshold. vLLM's docs also note disaggregated prefill does not improve throughput.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: NTFS and the master file table, record by record
question: Record 812 is marked free and its sequence number is 4. An entry in the NTFS change journal (lesson 6) refers to file reference 812 with sequence 3. What does that tell you?
options: The journal entry describes the same file that the record holds now
The journal is corrupt, because sequence numbers never change
Record 812 is a directory
The journal entry describes an earlier file that used record 812 before it was freed
explain: The sequence number increments each time a record is freed. Sequence 3 in the reference versus 4 in the record means the record has been freed since; the reference points to an older occupant.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: APFS: containers, copy-on-write and snapshots
question: You remove the internal SSD from an Apple silicon Mac with FileVault on and image it with a write-blocker. What do you have?
options: A readable APFS volume, because write-blockers bypass encryption
Encrypted data that stays unreadable without valid credentials or a recovery key
A blank image, because the SSD erases itself
A readable image as long as you image the whole container
explain: Apple documents that internal APFS volumes stay encrypted without valid login credentials or a cryptographic recovery key, even attached to another computer. A write-blocker preserves data; it does not decrypt it.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: SRUM and browser history: network use and what was visited
question: The suspect cleared their browser history. What can SRUM still offer?
options: Per-application, per-user network byte counts with timestamps, showing that the browser moved data
The URLs that were visited
The content of the uploaded file
Nothing, because clearing history also clears SRUM
explain: SRUM's Network Usage table records BytesSent and BytesRecvd per application and user. It does not record URLs or content, and the browser's clear-history function does not touch SRUDB.dat.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation
question: Which practice most directly addresses the risk that one tool misparses a crucial artefact?
options: Running the same tool twice
Using a newer computer
Hashing the report
Confirming the finding with an independent tool and against the raw data
explain: A second, independent implementation is unlikely to share the first tool's bug, and checking the raw bytes removes tool interpretation. Running the same tool repeats the same error; hashing the report only shows it did not change later.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: FreshDiskANN: inserts and deletes without rebuilds
question: In the toy consolidation, why do B's out-neighbors C and F become candidates for p?
options: Because they are p's nearest points
Because RobustPrune always adds every candidate
Because paths that ran p, B, C or p, B, F must be preserved by giving p a chance to link to them directly
Because C and F were on the DeleteList
explain: Algorithm 4 adds the deleted node's out-neighbors to the candidate set of each in-neighbor, so navigation through the hole is preserved. RobustPrune then decides which to keep: here C survives and F is covered by D.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
question: A pair has policy log-probs chosen -30, rejected -20 and reference log-probs chosen -32, rejected -18, with $\beta = 0.1$. What is the DPO margin, and does the implicit reward rank the pair correctly?
options: -1.0, ranked wrong, because the policy gives the chosen answer lower probability
+0.4, ranked correctly, even though the policy still gives the chosen answer lower probability
+1.0, ranked correctly
0, because the reference and policy disagree
explain: Chosen log-ratio: -30 - (-32) = +2. Rejected: -20 - (-18) = -2. Margin 0.1 x (2 - (-2)) = +0.4, so the implicit reward ranks it correctly. Yet the policy itself still prefers the rejected text (-20 beats -30). DPO scores improvement relative to the reference, not raw likelihood; lesson 5 shows why this matters.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
question: Dual writes have been on for a week, but the backfill has not run. A read from the new Subscriptions table for a customer who subscribed two years ago and has not changed since returns nothing. What happened?
options: The dual write to the new table failed for this customer
Nothing went wrong: untouched old objects only reach the new store through the backfill
The new table needs a read replica before it can serve reads
Dual writes copy old rows lazily on the first read, so the next read will succeed
explain: Dual writes only cover writes made after they were turned on. Stripe also copied objects lazily whenever they were *updated*, but an object nobody touches is copied only by the backfill. This is why reads must not move until the backfill and a completeness check are done.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
question: Midway through phase 3, the new write path for prorations is found to compute the wrong amount. Most other paths already write the new store first and archive to the old one. What is the safest response?
options: Restore the new store from last night's backup
Pause all writes until the bug is fixed
Delete the old store so the two cannot disagree
Flip the prorations path back to the old write order; the old store is still current because every path still writes it
explain: In phase 3 every write still reaches the old store (as the primary or as an archive), so it is complete. Rolling one path back by a flag is cheap. That safety disappears in phase 4, which is why it comes last.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: A read takes exactly 1,024 ns. In which hist() bucket does it appear?
explain: 1024 = 2^10, so b = 10 and the bucket is [2^10, 2^11) = [1K, 2K). Bucket intervals include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound; only 0 and 1 get single-value buckets.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
question: An activation tensor after ReLU has range [0, 6]. Using asymmetric int8 with q_min = -128, what are S and Z?
explain: S = (6 - 0) / (127 - (-128)) = 6/255 = 0.0235, and Z = round(-128 - 0/S) = -128. Real 0 maps to the lowest code, so all 256 levels cover [0, 6]. The symmetric choice (S = 6/127, Z = 0) would waste the 128 negative codes on values ReLU never produces.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
question: A wake-word model meets its accuracy target in float but loses 6 points after full-integer PTQ with per-channel weights. Calibration data is representative. What should you try next?
options: Quantization-aware training, or 16-bit activations if the runtime supports them
Per-tensor weights instead of per-channel
Remove calibration and use dynamic range quantization on a microcontroller with no float unit
Prune the model to 90% sparsity
explain: Per-channel weights and good calibration are already in place, so the remaining error likely comes from activations or from a small model's sensitivity. QAT lets the model adapt to rounding, and 16x8 mode reduces activation error. Per-tensor would be worse, and dynamic range keeps float outputs that an integer-only MCU cannot run.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
question: You installed the NetScaler fix on 11 October 2023, the day after it shipped. Why could an attacker still be using your gateway on 20 October?
options: The fix did not install
A session cookie stolen before the fix stayed valid until sessions were killed
The fix turned off MFA
NetScaler cannot be patched
explain: Exploitation began in late August. The fix stops new leaks but does not invalidate tokens already taken; NetScaler's guidance was to kill all active and persistent sessions after updating.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: The patch race: KEV-driven deadlines for edge devices
question: M-Trends 2026 estimates a mean time to exploit of -7 days. What does the negative sign mean for an edge patch process?
options: Patches arrive a week before bugs are found
On average, exploitation begins before a fix exists, so fast patching must be paired with checking for compromise that happened earlier
Attackers stopped using n-days
Vendors publish advisories a week late on purpose
explain: Negative TTE means exploitation precedes the patch. Speed still matters (it stops mass exploitation after disclosure), but forensic triage is what deals with the earlier window.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
question: Barracuda asked customers to replace ESG appliances 'regardless of patch version level'. What does that tell a defender about patching?
options: Patches from Barracuda were never released
Once an appliance may hold persistence the vendor cannot reliably remove, patching cannot restore trust; only new hardware can
Email gateways cannot be patched
Replacement is always cheaper than patching
explain: The patch fixed the bug, but the vendor could not be confident that software updates removed the intruder from compromised devices. The same logic drives rebuilds for Ivanti and hard resets for Cisco.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
question: A product needs answers under 1,500 output tokens from a reasoning model. Responses often come back incomplete with no visible text. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The model is refusing; rephrase the prompt
The output cap is cutting off hidden reasoning; lower the effort level (or thinking budget) and leave headroom in the cap
Temperature is too high; set it to 0
The cap counts only visible tokens, so raise it to the context length
explain: Reasoning tokens count toward the output limit. If the model plans a long think, a tight cap truncates it before the answer. Lowering effort changes the plan; the cap only stops it.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: AMSI in depth: what the scanner sees, and what it cannot
question: A script is downloaded as text, decoded twice in memory (Base64 then XOR) and run by PowerShell. Which content does AMSI receive?
options: The original downloaded text, exactly as it was on the wire
Only the file name of the script
Nothing: AMSI only scans files saved to disk
The decoded code PowerShell is about to run, after both layers are removed
explain: PowerShell calls AMSI with the code it is about to execute, after de-obfuscation. That is the design point: obfuscation must be undone before the engine can run the code, so the scan sees plain code.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: WMI: remote execution, event subscriptions and their telemetry
question: WMIC has been removed from your Windows 11 24H2 fleet. Does that remove WMI as a lateral movement channel?
options: Yes, WMI no longer works without WMIC
No: only the command-line tool is gone; WMI itself, reachable through PowerShell CIM cmdlets and other clients over DCOM or WinRM, is unchanged
Yes, because DCOM was removed at the same time
No, but WMI now only works locally
explain: Microsoft is explicit that the deprecation and removal apply only to the WMIC command-line utility and that WMI itself is not affected. Detection must still watch WmiPrvSE child processes and remote DCOM and WinRM traffic.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Credential hardening: LAPS, LSA protection and Credential Guard
question: A new Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise laptop joins the domain and meets the hardware requirements. Nobody configured Credential Guard. What is its likely state?
options: Off, it must always be enabled manually
Running by default, without UEFI lock
Running with UEFI lock that cannot be removed
Running only for local accounts
explain: Microsoft documents default enablement on Windows 11 22H2 and later for domain-joined, licensed devices meeting the requirements, unless explicitly disabled, and notes the default is without UEFI lock so admins can disable it remotely.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: XDR, MDR and running EDR well: the HSE lesson
question: Your EDR flags Mimikatz on a finance workstation at 02:00. Which response best matches the lessons of this course?
options: Email the server team in the morning
Isolate the device (it stays connected to the EDR service), collect an investigation package, and treat the user's and any cached admin credentials as compromised
Uninstall the EDR to stop the alerts
Wait to see whether ransomware follows
explain: Credential theft is the step before lateral movement. Isolation cuts the attacker's network path while keeping the device observable; credentials exposed on that host must be reset. Waiting is how HSE lost eight weeks.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
question: A seq2point model for the fridge is trained with W = 599 at 6-second samples. Which input does it use to predict fridge power at time t?
options: Only the mains sample at time t
About an hour of mains before time t only
About an hour of mains centred on time t, past and future
The fridge's own past power readings
explain: 599 samples x 6 s is about 60 minutes in total, roughly 30 minutes on each side of the midpoint. Seq2point is non-causal: it uses both past and future mains. It never sees sub-metered fridge data at test time, only the aggregate.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
question: City has m = 0.90 and u = 0.05 for exact agreement. A new data source has many members who typed their home city instead of the company's HQ city, so true duplicates agree on city only 45% of the time. What happens to the exact-city weight?
options: It stays 4.17 because u did not change
It drops to log2(0.45/0.05) = 3.17
It becomes negative
It doubles, because more disagreement means more information
explain: m measures how often true matches agree. Halving m from 0.90 to 0.45 subtracts exactly 1 from log2(m/u). Disagreement also becomes less damning: the else weight rises from log2(0.10/0.95) = -3.25 to log2(0.55/0.95) = -0.79.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
question: Why should emergency access accounts be cloud-only and not synced from on-premises AD?
options: Synced accounts cannot hold the Global Administrator role
So that an outage or compromise of on-premises AD or federation cannot block or take over the last way into the tenant
Because cloud-only accounts do not need MFA
Because PIM only works for cloud-only accounts
explain: Microsoft's guidance keeps emergency access for cloud and for on-premises separate, with no dependency between them. If they were synced or federated, the failure they exist for (federation down, AD compromised) would take them down too.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
question: An admin revokes a compromised user's sessions at 14:00. The attacker holds an access token for a third-party API (no CAE) issued at 13:50 with an 80-minute lifetime. Until when can the attacker call that API?
options: 15:10, when the access token expires
Indefinitely, because revocation only affects passwords
explain: Revocation invalidates refresh tokens and sessions at once, but an already-issued access token is checked only by the resource. Without CAE, the resource accepts it until expiry: 13:50 plus 80 minutes is 15:10.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
question: Your company buys a multitenant SaaS app and grants it an application permission. You license Workload ID Premium. Can a workload identity Conditional Access policy restrict where that app signs in from?
options: Yes, all service principals are covered
No: Microsoft documents that these policies cover only single-tenant service principals registered in your tenant, not multitenant or third-party SaaS apps
Only if the app is added to a group
Only for managed identities
explain: The documented scope is single-tenant service principals registered in your tenant. Multitenant SaaS apps and managed identities are excluded, and group-based assignment is not enforced, so control those apps through their grants and reviews.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A hardening baseline, an incident runbook, and where to practise
question: After a full on-premises AD compromise, an organisation rebuilds Entra ID security (new admins, revoked sessions) but leaves Entra Connect, PTA agents and the AZUREADSSOACC key as they were. What is the risk?
options: None: the cloud was rebuilt
Re-compromise: whoever still controls the Tier 0 bridges can change synced users, sit in password checks or forge Seamless SSO tickets
Only that sync will slow down
Only guest users are affected
explain: Lesson 11's bridges create or impersonate cloud identities. Until the sync accounts, agents and Seamless SSO key are reset from a clean AD, the attacker keeps a path back into the tenant.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
question: A level-triggered server registers every connection with EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT and leaves it that way. CPU sits at 100 percent even with no traffic. Why?
options: EPOLLOUT is invalid without EPOLLET
Idle sockets almost always have send-buffer space, so each one is reported writable on every epoll_wait and the loop never sleeps
epoll_wait ignores the timeout when EPOLLOUT is set
The kernel rescans the interest list on every call
explain: Level-triggered means "report while the condition holds". Writable is true for nearly every idle socket, so every wait returns immediately with work that is not real. Register EPOLLOUT only while you have unsent data (EPOLL_CTL_MOD), or use ET.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
question: Why does the MS MARCO document leaderboard score every submission on 45 extra queries that never appear on the public board?
options: To give the organizers a held-out check on whether public gains carry over to queries no one could tune on
To raise the total number of evaluation queries so the public score is more precise
Because TREC labels are too expensive to show publicly
To break ties on the public leaderboard
explain: A private set that no participant receives feedback on cannot be adaptively overfit. If teams were climbing the public board by tuning to its queries, their runs would gain publicly and slip on the private queries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
question: A program is built with NX but not with a stack canary. An overflow replaces the return address with the address of the overflowing buffer itself, which holds attacker bytes. What happens at ret?
options: The injected bytes run, because NX only protects the heap
The return address is restored by NX
ret jumps to the stack, the CPU refuses to execute from a non-executable page, and the process faults
The compiler refuses to compile the overflow
explain: NX does not prevent the hijack; it prevents the hijacked jump from running data. The process faults on the instruction fetch from the stack page. The return address was still corrupted, which is why attackers moved to reusing code that is already executable (next lesson).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Control-flow integrity: checking where indirect calls land
question: Microsoft CFG allows an indirect call to any function that is a valid indirect-call target. A corrupted function pointer in a Windows program is changed to point at the start of another such function. What happens?
options: CFG terminates the process because the type differs
NX blocks the call
ASLR moves the function so the call misses
The call is allowed: CFG checks the entry point is valid, not that it is the intended function
explain: CFG is coarse-grained: it rejects calls into the middle of functions or to non-code, but any registered entry point passes. Type-based schemes such as Clang cfi-icall narrow this further, and no CFI scheme can choose between two valid targets of the same type.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
question: After Android 7, an attacker achieves code execution in libstagefright through a new parsing bug. What do they most likely still need to read the user's camera?
options: Nothing: libstagefright still runs in mediaserver
Only the camera permission from the app manifest
A way around the integer-overflow sanitizer
A second bug to escape the mediacodec sandbox or to attack cameraserver, which alone may use the camera
explain: The parser now runs in a sandbox that SELinux denies camera access. Camera use is confined to cameraserver, so the attacker needs another vulnerability: the containment goal of the redesign.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
question: Which access pattern causes the most coherence traffic on one 64-byte line?
options: Eight threads each read a different 8-byte field
One thread repeatedly writes all eight fields
Two threads on different cores each write their own field
Eight threads read the same field
explain: Reads leave the line Shared in every cache with no ongoing traffic. A single writer keeps the line Modified in its own cache with no one to invalidate. Two writers on different cores each need an RFO before each write after the other one wrote, so the line ping-pongs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
question: Eight hospitals want one shared model and no record may leave any hospital. What is the training objective?
options: Each hospital trains alone and the best of the eight models is shipped
The same pooled average loss as centralized training, written as a sum of per-hospital losses weighted by record count
The unweighted mean of the eight per-hospital losses, since each hospital is one client
A new objective that no centralized training run could express
explain: Federated learning changes who computes, not what is being minimized. The objective is the pooled average loss, which factors exactly into a sum over clients with weights n_k/n. The unweighted mean is a different objective: it would give a hospital with 200 records the same influence as one with 20000.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum
question: You need 200 reporting devices per round and measure an 8 percent dropout rate. How many should you invite, and what happens to the extras?
options: Exactly 200, and retry the ones that fail inside the same round
About 260 (130 percent), closing the round once 200 have reported and aborting the rest
As many as check in, aggregating every update that ever arrives
400, so that a full round survives even if half the devices vanish
explain: Over-selecting by about 130 percent is the deployed practice: it absorbs the 6 to 10 percent that drop out and lets the slowest tail be discarded. The round closes on the quorum, and the surplus tail gets aborted, which is why 22 percent of sessions in the measured population finished training but had their result rejected.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
question: A team has an existing HNSW index over 500M vectors and cannot afford a long rebuild. Which approach fits best?
options: ACORN-gamma with gamma = 1/s_min
ACORN-1 style two-hop lookups over a standard HNSW-like graph
StitchedVamana with one graph per label
Raise M in the existing HNSW and rebuild
explain: ACORN-1 needs no expanded lists at build time; it reconstructs a denser neighborhood during search. Weaviate took this route: its blog says it kept vanilla HNSW indexing so existing data does not need re-indexing. ACORN-gamma and StitchedVamana both require heavier construction, and raising M flattens the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Shared experts: an always-on path for common knowledge
question: A team configures 2 shared + 64 routed quarter-size experts and routes to 8 routed experts, keeping the same 2 shared. Compared with DeepSeekMoE 16B (2 + 6 active), what changed?
options: Nothing; shared experts do not count toward compute
Total parameters rose by 2 experts
Activated expert compute rose from 8 to 10 quarter-experts, i.e. from 2 to 2.5 standard FFNs per token
Only the router cost changed
explain: Shared experts always run, so they count fully toward activated compute. DeepSeekMoE lowers the routed top-K by $K_s$ to keep compute fixed: 2 + 6 = 8 quarter-size experts = 2 FFNs. Using 2 + 8 means 10 quarters = 2.5 FFNs, 25% more expert FLOPs.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: MoE on real hardware: expert parallelism, all-to-all and serving
question: A team switches from 64 experts with top-2 to 256 experts with top-8, each a quarter as wide, keeping active parameters fixed. A step routes 2048 tokens. How many rows does each expert's GEMM get on average, and what changes?
options: 16 rows after the switch, because 4 times as many experts share the tokens
256 rows after the switch, because top-8 sends 4 times as many copies of each token
Nothing changes, because FLOPs per token are equal
64 rows in both designs (2048 x 2 / 64 and 2048 x 8 / 256), so intensity stays near 60, but there are 4 times as many GEMMs, each a quarter the size, and each token goes to 4 times as many experts
explain: Tokens per expert = B x K / N, and K and N both grew 4 times. Rows per expert stay at 64, so each GEMM is still memory-bound at the same intensity, but the same work is now split over 4 times as many smaller launches and dispatch destinations. Fine granularity costs efficiency unless kernels group the experts and batches grow.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 forward: when the exponential is the bottleneck
question: Why does FlashAttention-4 emulate only 10 to 25% of exponentials in software instead of all of them?
options: The polynomial is too inaccurate for more than a quarter of the row
Emulation uses extra registers, register bandwidth and latency; doing all of them would cause spills and leave MUFU idle
FMA units can only process one row in four
MUFU is faster than the FMA units for every input
explain: The goal is to split the work between two units that can run in parallel. The paper says full emulation would raise register pressure and could cause spills that cancel the gain, so the fraction is tuned to the MMA-to-exp ratio of each tile shape. Accuracy is not the limit: after BF16 rounding the polynomial matches hardware.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Attention states, cascade attention and composable formats
question: Partial states for one query: prefix $(O = 2.0, \mathrm{LSE} = 0)$ and suffix $(O = 6.0, \mathrm{LSE} = 0)$. What is the merged output?
options: 6.0, the larger LSE wins
It cannot be computed without the raw scores
explain: Equal LSEs mean both halves carry equal total softmax mass, so the weights are $e^0/(e^0+e^0) = 0.5$ each and $O = 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0.5 \cdot 6 = 4.0$. The merged LSE is $\log 2$. The states alone are enough; that is the whole point of the operator.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
question: Which statement about conditional flow matching is correct?
options: It needs the marginal velocity field computed over the whole dataset at every step
It only works with straight-line paths
Regressing onto per-sample conditional velocities gives the same gradient as regressing onto the intractable marginal velocity
It trains by maximizing the log-likelihood of the data under the ODE
explain: Lipman et al. Theorem 2: the CFM and FM losses differ by a constant independent of the parameters, so their gradients match. Straight OT paths are one choice; diffusion-style Gaussian paths also fit the framework.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
question: A race fires in 1 of every 184,756 equally likely orders. Your CI runs the test 1,000 times a day, each run picking an order at random. Which statement is closest to right?
options: Over a week you have roughly a 4% chance of having seen the bug even once
After a week of green runs the code is very likely correct
The bug is impossible in practice because its probability is so small
Running the test on more cores makes the bug certain to appear
explain: 7,000 runs give $1-(1-1/184756)^{7000} \approx 3.7\%$. Green CI says little here. Rare orders still happen in production, where the same code runs billions of times; AWS noted that improbability is not a defense against such bugs.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Modeling a distributed protocol: messages, loss and duplication
question: Why does TwoPhase.tla need no Lose action to check safety?
options: TLC assumes a reliable network unless told otherwise
Message loss cannot break safety in any protocol
Sets automatically drop messages at random
No action is ever forced to receive a message, so a lost message looks the same as one that is never received
explain: Safety specs only allow steps, they never require them. A behavior in which nobody reads a message is already included, and that is exactly what loss looks like. Loss matters for liveness, where fairness would otherwise force the receive.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Ghost permissions, VerusSync and what a proof trusts
question: Your team is designing a new lease-based leader handoff for a replicated store and has two weeks. Where should formal effort go first?
options: A TLA+ spec of the handoff protocol with crashes and message loss, model checked with 3 nodes
Verus proofs of every Rust function in the storage engine
TLAPS proofs of liveness
Nothing formal; add more integration tests
explain: Design bugs in protocols are the cheapest to find with a model checker, and a wrong design makes correct code pointless. AWS's experience: specs of a few hundred lines found bugs in weeks. Code proofs cost several proof lines per code line, and TLAPS liveness proofs need hand-written fairness and temporal reasoning, far more effort than a model check.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
question: Two data-parallel ranks quantize their gradients to FP8 with their own per-tensor scales and run a standard all-reduce on the raw FP8 values. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because all-reduce is a sum and sums commute
The all-reduce overflows on every step
NCCL rejects FP8 tensors
The summed values mix two different scales, so no single scale decodes the sum correctly
explain: Each stored value means value divided by its own rank's scale. Adding 3 (scale 1000) and 12 (scale 4000) gives 15, which decodes to neither 0.006 nor anything meaningful. FP8-LM all-reduces the minimum scale first, requantizes, and only then sums.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4
question: In part 5 the output error stayed near 13.5% from K = 256 to K = 4096. Which change would make output error grow with K?
options: Using a larger random seed
Replacing round-to-nearest with stochastic rounding on both inputs
Using 32-value blocks instead of 16
Summing the products in a 14-bit float instead of float64, so each add onto a growing sum loses its low bits
explain: Input rounding errors scale with the signal. Random-sign errors grow like sqrt(K), as the signal of random data does; a one-way bias grows like K, but so does the signal of same-sign data, so the ratio stays flat. What grows with K is the accumulator: lesson 3's 14-bit running sum adds each product onto an ever coarser grid, which is why DeepSeek promotes partial sums to FP32.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Group commit: one WAL flush makes many transactions durable
question: A WAL device needs 4 ms per flush and is busy flushing all the time. On average each flush carries 10 commit records. What is the commit throughput?
options: 250 commits/s
2,500 commits/s
40 commits/s
25,000 commits/s
explain: X = B / F = 10 / 0.004 s = 2,500 commits/s. Without sharing (B = 1) the same device tops out at 250/s.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Fuzzing from a stormy night in 1988: random, mutation, generation
question: What did Miller's original fuzz study use as its oracle?
options: A specification of each utility's correct output
Code coverage reached by each input
A comparison with a second implementation
Whether the program crashed or hung
explain: The oracle was deliberately simple: crash or hang means fail. That is why it could be automated across many programs and operating systems with no model of what each program should do.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Sanitizers as oracles: which bug each one catches
question: The TSan run printed hits = 200000, the correct total. Why is the report still a real bug?
options: It is not; the output proves the code is correct
TSan always reports false positives on counters
The total is only correct because of TSan
A race is undefined behaviour; this run got lucky, other compilers, optimisation levels or timings can lose updates
explain: TSan reports the unsynchronised access itself, not a wrong answer. Correct output on one run proves nothing about the next one, which is exactly why a race detector beats checking results.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed
question: How was Cloudbleed actually discovered?
options: A fuzzer crashed Cloudflare's edge servers
Cloudflare's monitoring alerted on high memory use
A customer reported a wrong page
Data gathered for fuzzing corpora contained leaked memory that did not match what Tavis Ormandy expected
explain: Ormandy's Project Zero report describes a corpus distillation project: public data collected to build fuzzing corpora contained uninitialised memory. Fuzzing infrastructure found it, but not by crashing anything.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Variant analysis and patch diffing: one bug, many siblings
question: Why did fuzzing find new Bash bugs after the first Shellshock patch?
options: The patch introduced them
AFL is better than code review at all bugs
The bugs were in a different program
The first patch only blocked one symptom; the function-import parser, still reachable from untrusted environment variables, had more bugs that AFL's coverage feedback explored
explain: Zalewski's write-up: AFL derived about 1,000 distinct test cases from one seed function definition and found CVE-2014-6277 and 6278 in the same parser. The robust fix stopped untrusted variables from reaching it.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
question: You only accept matches with at most 1 edit. The query has 6 characters and a candidate has 9. How much of the DP table must you fill to reject the candidate?
options: All 7 x 10 cells
Only the diagonal band of width 3
None: the length difference already proves the distance is at least 3
Only the last row
explain: Every character of length difference needs at least one insertion or deletion, so $d \ge 9-6 = 3 > 1$. A length check is the cheapest filter of all and real implementations apply it before touching the table.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
question: SymSpell with k = 1 finds that the query and a dictionary word share a one-character delete, while neither is a delete of the other. What kind of single error explains that?
options: An insertion in the query
A deletion in the query
A substitution or an adjacent transposition
Nothing; it is a false positive that cannot be within 1 edit
explain: A shared one-character delete fits one differing position (a substitution, like reieve from recieve and relieve) or an adjacent swap (receve from recieve and receive). It does not guarantee 1 edit: abc and bca share the delete bc but are 2 edits apart, so SymSpell verifies every candidate with a real distance.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Searching code space: kd-trees, tolerance and why quads beat triangles
question: Why did quint (5-star) indexes solve images more slowly than quads, even though a quint match is almost always correct?
options: 6D kd-tree lookups are impossible
The solver must try many quints before finding one whose 5 stars are all in both the image and the index, and higher-dimensional search is slower
Quint codes are not scale invariant
Quints produce more coincidental matches than triangles
explain: The paper reports that for over 80% of solved images the first quint match found was correct. The cost is elsewhere: the chance that all 5 stars are detected and catalogued is lower, so many more quints are tried, and near-neighbor search slows with dimension.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
question: Which statement about two geohashes is always true?
options: If both points share a 6-character prefix at the equator, they are at most about 1.35 km apart
If two points are less than 100 m apart, they share at least a 5-character prefix
Geohashes that are adjacent in sort order are always in adjacent cells
Two points with no shared prefix are at least 1,000 km apart
explain: A shared 6-character prefix means both points are in one cell of 1.2 km x 609.4 m, whose diagonal is about 1.35 km. The other statements fail at cell boundaries: the London pair is 69 m apart with no shared prefix, and the Z-order curve jumps between quadrants.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Pixels in memory: NHWC, NCHW, pitch and a warp's 96 bytes
question: A color-convert kernel reads an RGB8 (uchar3) NHWC image with one pixel per thread. Why is the per-instruction load efficiency about 33 percent?
options: The image rows are not padded, so the second row starts unaligned
Each channel load has stride 3 across lanes, so its sectors carry three times the bytes that one instruction uses
NHWC always loses to NCHW because planes are contiguous
A warp of 32 threads cannot cover 96 bytes in fewer than 32 transactions
explain: A uchar3 has alignment 1, so a pixel is three separate 1-byte accesses. Each of those instructions touches 32 addresses that are 3 bytes apart, spanning 96 bytes of sectors to deliver 32 useful bytes. The warp's total footprint is still contiguous, which is why the fix is a wider access (a 4-pixel carrier or an RGBA8 format), not a different layout.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo
question: A 16x16 block computing one output per thread stages a tile for a 9x9 filter. How large is the tile, and how much of it is halo?
options: 16x16 = 256 elements, no halo, because shared memory is indexed per thread
25x25 = 625 elements, of which 369 are halo
24x24 = 576 elements, of which 320 are halo: 2.25 loads per output
32x32 = 1024 elements, rounded up to the warp size
explain: The tile is (16 + 9 - 1) square = 24x24 = 576 elements for 256 outputs, so 320 halo elements and 2.25 loads per output. The halo is k - 1 = 8 elements across both dimensions together, not k, because a radius-4 window needs 4 extra on each side.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
question: Tensor A is allocated on s0, read by a kernel on s1, then deleted without record_stream. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; the allocator always waits for all streams before reuse
The allocator raises an error because A was used on two streams
The block leaks and is never reused
s0 can reuse A's block for a new tensor while s1's kernel is still reading it
explain: Without record_stream the allocator only knows about s0. Reuse on s0 is ordered after s0's work, but nothing orders it after s1's kernel, so the new tensor can overwrite data s1 is still using.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
question: A row-major `float` matrix has `ld = 4096` columns. A kernel with 32 x 32 blocks computes `int r = blockIdx.y*32 + threadIdx.x; int c = blockIdx.x*32 + threadIdx.y;` and reads `a[r*ld + c]`. How many sectors does each warp load request?
options: 4, because the warp reads 32 floats
8, because the matrix is large
1, because all threads share c
32, because consecutive threads are 4096 floats apart
explain: Within a warp threadIdx.y is fixed and threadIdx.x runs 0 to 31, so it is r that varies. Consecutive threads are ld = 4096 floats (16 KB) apart, each in its own sector: 32 sectors per request and 12.5% efficiency. Swapping which index uses threadIdx.x fixes it.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
question: A colleague reports: "Nsight Systems says the GPU is 97 percent utilized, so the GPU is the bottleneck and we need better kernels." What is the hole in that reasoning?
options: Nothing: 97 percent time utilization means the SMs are 97 percent busy
Utilization there is time based, so a long exposed memcpy or a tiny kernel occupying one SM counts as full utilization
Nsight Systems cannot measure GPU utilization at all, only CPU time
It is wrong only if the application uses more than one CUDA stream
explain: The rule's own notes say the utilization is time utilization, not resource utilization: a single running memcpy counts the same as a huge kernel, and concurrent operations can sum past 100 percent. 97 percent busy could be 97 percent copying, or one kernel with a 1-block grid. Per-kernel counters, not timeline utilization, tell you whether the hardware is actually being used.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
question: Which single profiling decision most often invalidates a comparison between two versions of a kernel?
options: Changing the capture configuration between the two runs, for example clock, cache or replay settings
Profiling on a GPU that has a display attached
Using the basic section set instead of the full one
Reporting durations in microseconds rather than milliseconds
explain: Both the triage guide and the profiling guide insist on it: keep capture settings stable while comparing runs, and keep cache-control and replay settings identical unless the policy itself is the variable under test. A display-attached GPU adds noise and a smaller section set loses detail, but a changed control turns a measurement into an incomparable one.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
question: Which barrier placement is valid?
options: `if (blockIdx.x % 2 == 0) { __syncthreads(); }`
`if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0) { __syncthreads(); }`
`if (threadIdx.x < 64) { __syncthreads(); }`
`for (int k = 0; k < threadIdx.x; ++k) __syncthreads();`
explain: blockIdx.x is the same for every thread in a block, so the condition is uniform across the block and either all of its threads reach the barrier or none do. The other three depend on threadIdx, so some threads of the block skip or repeat the barrier: undefined behavior.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
question: Community X has internal weight $L_X = 4$ and degree sum $k_X = 12$ in a graph with $m = 20$. What is its modularity term?
explain: $L_X/m = 4/20 = 0.20$ and $(k_X/2m)^2 = (12/40)^2 = 0.09$, so the term is 0.11. Dividing by $m$ rather than $2m$ in the second term is the common slip.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
question: FastGraphRAG builds relationships from co-occurrence instead of LLM extraction. What do you lose?
options: Community detection, which then cannot run
Relationship and entity descriptions; edges only say that two noun phrases appeared in the same text unit, so the graph is noisier
The ability to answer global questions at all
All embeddings
explain: The docs say FastGraphRAG has no entity or relationship descriptions and a noisier graph. Leiden and community reports still run, which is why it remains useful for global summary questions.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: The GRPO objective token by token: clipping, averaging and KL
question: Why does GRPO put the KL penalty in the loss rather than subtracting it from the reward like PPO for RLHF?
options: The KL in the loss is cheaper to compute
Folding a per-token KL into the reward would mix it into the group-normalized advantage, which is meant to be a pure comparison of sibling rewards
The reward cannot be negative
PPO's KL estimator is biased
explain: DeepSeekMath says adding the KL to the loss avoids complicating the advantage calculation. GRPO has no critic to spread a per-token reward over the sequence; its advantage is one standardized outcome per output.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: RLOO, GSPO, off-policy drift, and what RLVR teaches
question: A team training a large MoE model with GRPO sees token ratios swing wildly between minibatch updates even at a small learning rate, and training collapses. Which change targets that cause?
options: Raise beta so the KL term holds the policy back
Switch to sequence-level ratios and clipping (GSPO), or replay the old expert routing when recomputing ratios
Increase the group size G from 8 to 64
Divide advantages by the response length
explain: The GSPO paper traces the swings to expert routing changing after each update, so per-token ratios compare different sub-networks. Routing Replay fixes the ratios by reusing the old routing; GSPO avoids depending on per-token likelihoods at all.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
question: A consumer joins TripUpdates to the schedule using only trip_id. For a daily train with trip_id N8 departing 20:00, the producer sends an update for yesterday's N8, now running 14 hours late. What breaks?
options: Nothing, delays over 12 hours are discarded by protobuf
The feed is rejected because delay must be under 3600 s
The update cannot be applied because it has no stop_id
The update is applied to today's N8, so riders see a wrong prediction
explain: Without start_date the consumer cannot tell yesterday's instance from today's. The reference requires start_date exactly when such collisions are possible. Always key realtime state by (trip_id, start_date) and, for frequency trips, start_time.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
question: You need an accurate L1 miss ratio, but you also asked perf for 10 other events, and every line shows about (40%). What is the best fix?
options: Run longer, since scaling error always averages out
Multiply both counts by 2.5 yourself
Put the two L1 events in one group with braces, or measure them in a run of their own
Switch to sampling mode with perf record
explain: Grouped events are scheduled together, so both counts cover the same instructions and their ratio is valid even if the group is multiplexed. Running longer does not fix phase-dependent bias, and scaling by hand is what perf already does.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Timing attacks on RSA: Kocher 1996 and remote timing in 2003
question: Kocher's attack learns exponent bit b. What must the attacker already know to do that?
options: Bits 0 to b-1, so they can simulate the computation up to bit b
The full private key, to check the result
Nothing: each bit is measured independently
The random blinding factor
explain: Knowing the earlier bits lets the attacker compute the exact intermediate value and so predict the time of the next optional multiplication. Each bit learned enables the next one.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Out-of-order and speculative execution, from zero
question: Why do CPUs speculate at all, given these risks?
options: To save power when idle
Because the C standard requires it
Because waiting for every slow load before continuing would leave the core idle for hundreds of cycles at a time
To make branch prediction possible
explain: A miss to DRAM costs hundreds of cycles; a correct guess lets the core do useful work during the wait. That is the performance the whole industry built on, as the Spectre paper notes.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: The family grows: Foreshadow, MDS, Downfall, Zenbleed, Inception
question: Why do several of these mitigations mention SMT (hyperthreading)?
options: SMT threads have separate caches
SMT makes speculation impossible
Sibling hyperthreads share the core's L1 cache, buffers and register file, so an attacker on one sibling can sample data from the other while it runs
Hypervisors cannot run with SMT on
explain: Clearing buffers on a context switch does not help when the attacker runs at the same time on the sibling thread. Hence options such as auto,nosmt and core scheduling.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
question: The Linux kernel's hardware embargo process asks for embargoes to be as short as possible. Which reason does its documentation give?
options: Long embargoes force developers to keep private patches up to date with ongoing kernel development, creating extra work and conflicts
Shorter embargoes make CVEs cheaper
Hardware vendors prefer short embargoes
Researchers cannot publish papers during an embargo
explain: The document says extending embargoes for non-technical reasons such as conference dates creates more work and burden, because patches must keep tracking upstream changes.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: With the defaults, what does setting khugepaged/max_ptes_none to 0 trade away?
options: Faults no longer allocate huge pages
khugepaged will not collapse any range with even one unpopulated PTE, so sparse regions stay on 4 KiB pages but never bloat
Huge pages can no longer be swapped
khugepaged stops running
explain: max_ptes_none only governs collapse: at 0, a range must have all 512 PTEs populated. That removes collapse-induced bloat but fewer ranges become huge. Fault-time allocation is controlled by enabled and defrag, not this knob.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Measure recall yourself: MQAR and a tiny hybrid in code
question: Why does MQAR separate a recurrent model from attention more sharply than a test with a single query at the end?
options: A single query lets the model store little; with many queries at different times, every pair must stay retrievable at once
MQAR sequences are much longer, and recurrent models cannot run on long sequences
MQAR uses a larger vocabulary, which recurrent models cannot embed
With one query, attention cannot find the key
explain: With one question at the end, a recurrent model can in principle get by with whatever survived in its state. MQAR asks about every pair, in an order the model cannot predict, so all of them must be held simultaneously in the fixed state. Attention just looks each one up.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
question: A team must cut KV memory but keeps exact recall at 200K tokens. Which design is riskiest?
options: 1 full attention layer per 8 layers, Mamba-2 elsewhere
Mamba layers plus only 2048-token sliding window attention
Gated DeltaNet with a full attention layer every 4 layers
Parallel attention and SSM heads with global attention in the first, middle and last layers
explain: With only sliding window attention, no layer can look up a token 200K positions back exactly; that recall must survive inside the fixed Mamba state. The other three keep at least a few global attention layers that can read the whole KV cache.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Convex combination: normalize, then weight with alpha
question: After min-max normalization, a query whose dense results all have cosine 0.80 to 0.81 gets dense scores spread from 0 to 1. What is the risk?
options: None; normalization makes scores comparable by design
Cosine scores become negative
Tiny, possibly meaningless cosine differences are stretched to the full range and can outweigh real BM25 differences
BM25 scores are rescaled to match the cosine range
explain: Min-max always maps the list's min to 0 and max to 1, regardless of how close they were. Our toy shows a milder version: a 0.11 cosine range became 0 to 1. Theoretical min-max (dividing from the known lower bound, -1 for cosine) keeps such near-ties close.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
question: You normalize the HyDE mean vector to length 1 before searching an inner-product index. What happens to the top-10 results?
options: They stay the same; only the score values change
They change, because longer vectors favor longer documents
They improve, because cosine is always better than inner product
They get worse, because the query contribution is removed
explain: Dividing the query vector by its positive length scales every document's score by the same factor, so the ordering is identical. Document vectors are untouched, so this is not the same as switching the whole index from inner product to cosine.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Inside a plant: sensors, PLCs, RTUs, HMIs, historians and SIS
question: A refinery's safety system is designed so that it can still shut the unit down even if the main control system has crashed. Which design property is this?
options: Redundancy of the historian
Independence of the SIS from the BPCS
Real-time scheduling of the HMI
Remote access to field sites
explain: NIST describes the SIS as often independent from other control systems so that a BPCS failure does not harm SIS function. That independence is exactly what attackers in the Triton case worked to get around.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Modbus/TCP byte by byte, and why it trusts everyone
question: A server replies with function code 0x83 and one data byte 0x02. What happened?
options: A successful read of 2 registers
A new function code 0x83 the server supports
A write of value 2
An exception to a Read Holding Registers (03) request, with exception code 2
explain: Exception replies set the high bit: 0x80 + 0x03 = 0x83. Exception code 02 is 'illegal data address' in the spec. A burst of exceptions often means someone is probing addresses.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
question: Why did ESET judge Industroyer more dangerous than the 2015 toolset?
options: It encrypted files for ransom
It was signed with stolen certificates
It spread by USB
It implemented four industrial protocols itself, so it could command switches and breakers directly without the operators' software
